source.title: Shattered Compositionality: Counterintuitive Learning Dynamics of Transformers for Arithmetic
source.authors: Xing-Yu Zhao; Darsh Sharma; Rheeya Uppaal; Yi-Qiao Zhong

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites grokking work as related background but does not test delayed generalization after overfitting or rely on grokking as a method. Its own arithmetic-learning results concern different learning dynamics and do not measure the behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports arithmetic skill-acquisition trajectories and robustness results, but does not report the train-accuracy saturation, chance-level test accuracy, and late test-accuracy rise required by V1. Its MI analysis does not track a generalizing circuit or memorizing components, and it does not test the other version-specific mechanisms or claims. The related arithmetic-learning results are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper cites grokking (Power et al., Nanda et al.) only as related work. Its experiments track digit-wise subskill acquisition order in transformers trained on large synthetic arithmetic datasets (1M addition, 100K multiplication examples). It reports no train-accuracy saturation followed by a delayed test-accuracy jump and no training-set-size sweep. It identifies no generalizing or memorizing circuit, and it does not vary weight norm, initialization scale, optimizer or numerical precision. The sharp training-loss drops aligned with mutual-information matching are phase transitions in training loss, not generalization after overfitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: transformers learn arithmetic subskills in reverse or parallel order ('shattered compositionality'), shaped by correlational matching to the training data. This causes skill competition, mixing errors and brittleness under shift, and the pattern is not fixed by scaling or scratchpads.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformers on synthetic arithmetic and measures digit-wise skill acquisition, mutual-information patterns, and robustness. It does not reproduce the original grokking train/test accuracy setup or its dataset-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning trajectories vary with output format and scratchpad format. The qualitative non-human digit order is reported across several positional encodings, output permutations, decoding schemes, and random seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformers acquire addition digits from most to least significant, regardless of output format, positional encoding, seed, model scale (20M, 100M), Pythia-1B fine-tuning or scratchpad. Multiplication shows bidirectional acquisition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers acquire arithmetic subskills in non-human orders shaped by correlational structure in the data.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharp training-loss drops coincide with model predictions matching the data's conditional mutual information. Randomizing the thousands-place output keeps lower-place errors near random baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stagewise loss drops in arithmetic training track the availability of correlational signals.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallel subskill acquisition produces temporary non-monotone errors in comparison and mixing errors in sorting: 6.63% on conflicting cues vs 3.61% on agreeing cues.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parallel subskill acquisition causes competition and brittleness under shift.

fits_no_version.finding: All 10 evaluated LLMs lose accuracy as clauses are added to GSM8K-derived questions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained LLMs are brittle to increased multi-operand composition.

record.problems: The paper's main arithmetic results are not tests of grokking as defined in the claim: the required train/test accuracy timing and training-set-size comparison are not reported. Many trajectories are presented in figures without numerical summaries or uncertainty estimates. The modern-LLM evaluation has 50 curated templates, and the paper notes that it does not establish that LLMs use the same mechanisms as the small transformers.
record.rows_left_out: Other robustness checks and appendix results were not included because they repeat the reported qualitative acquisition-order pattern or concern additional sorting error analyses rather than a distinct result needed for the claim record.

untested.parts: No train/test gap timing on small algorithmic datasets and no dataset-size dependence of any delay.
No circuit or memorization-component analysis. The MI metrics track input-output dependence in predictions, not a generalizing circuit anticipating a grokking jump.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Pythia-1B fine-tuning and evaluation of 10 trained LLMs on clause-extended GSM8K, but no delayed generalization measured.
Weight decay is fixed at 0.1 and never varied. No critical dataset size or ungrokking is tested.
Seeds and architectures show the same qualitative digit learning order, but no algorithm is identified or compared across runs.
AdamW is used throughout. Optimizer instability and softmax precision are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (cites_only, T6) and all versions-['none'] row links are correct. The phase transitions here concern training loss and digit acquisition with large datasets, not delayed test generalization. R9/R10 baseline (1.7%) is the final in-distribution test error, which is acceptable as context.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report train accuracy saturating while test accuracy remains at chance and later rises, or whether delay increases as training data shrinks.
Does not identify a generalizing circuit or memorizing components, or test whether circuit formation anticipates a grokking jump.
Does not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic training data or control delays through initialization scale, weight norm, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
Modern LLMs are evaluated on a clause-extended benchmark, but the paper does not measure delayed generalization during their pretraining or fine-tuning.
Does not test a low-norm efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.

Different seeds are tested for qualitative learning-order consistency, but the paper does not identify algorithms or establish that runs converge to the same algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point limits in the softmax as causes of grokking.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on four-operand addition and track digit-wise error during training.
rows.value: Models learn from higher-place digits toward lower-place digits; the plain-output model converges faster overall than the reverse-output model.
rows.note: Qualitative result described by the authors; this is a subskill-acquisition trajectory, not a train/test grokking measurement.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on four-operand addition and track digit-wise error during training.
rows.value: The model still learns higher-place digits first rather than following the lower-to-higher order encouraged by the output format; the authors report sharper phase transitions.
rows.note: The paper reports digit-wise learning order, not the claimed delayed test-accuracy rise.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Track mutual information between input digits and model prediction distributions during addition training.
rows.measure: Model-prediction mutual information compared with training-data mutual information, alongside training loss
rows.baseline: Corresponding mutual-information structure in the training data
rows.value: The authors report that sharp training-loss descents coincide with the model predictions matching the data mutual-information structure at output digits.
rows.note: This is an information-theoretic account of digit-skill acquisition, not a measurement of a generalizing circuit or memorizing components.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on addition after replacing the thousands-place target digit with a uniformly sampled digit.
rows.baseline: Random baselines shown for digit predictions
rows.value: Even after hundreds of thousands of training steps, most lower-place error rates remain near random baseline.
rows.note: The intervention tests dependence among digit skills, not delayed generalization after overfitting.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on simple multiplication and track digit-wise error during training.

conditions.value: up to 40-digit number times one digit

rows.value: Learning proceeds from the most significant end while the units-place digit is acquired early in parallel.
rows.note: The authors describe bidirectional acquisition rather than a single sequential order.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on simple multiplication and track digit-wise error during training.

conditions.value: up to 40-digit number times one digit

rows.value: Learning proceeds from the most significant end while the units-place digit is acquired early in parallel.
rows.note: The authors report the same bidirectional acquisition pattern for the reverse output format.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on number comparison and evaluate contrast pairs that differ at one digit position.

conditions.value: four contrast-pair groups, one per digit position

rows.measure: Error rate on contrast pairs over training
rows.value: The thousands-place group shows a temporary increase in errors when the model begins learning to predict equality; the authors report temporary non-monotonicity and later reconciliation.
rows.note: This measures temporary competition among comparison subskills.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Train on sorting and track acquisition of length and digit-wise subskills.
rows.value: The model learns crude length early, then learns the four digit-wise skills concurrently; the fourth digit lags behind.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate sorting examples with conflicting comparison cues.
rows.note: The paper compares this shifted-test condition with the agreeing condition and final test error.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate sorting examples with agreeing comparison cues.
rows.note: The authors report more mixing errors for the conflicting group than for this agreeing group.

rows.subject: NanoGPT, 20M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Scale the NanoGPT model and train it on four-operand addition.
rows.value: The model exhibits the same qualitative reverse digit-wise learning order as the baseline.
rows.locator: Figure 7(a), Figure 27(a); Section 5.2 and Appendix E.1
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative order, not a grokking measure.

rows.subject: NanoGPT, 100M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Scale the NanoGPT model and train it on four-operand addition.
rows.value: The model exhibits the same qualitative reverse digit-wise learning order as the baseline.
rows.locator: Figure 7(b), Figure 27(b); Section 5.2 and Appendix E.1
rows.note: The appendix says learning iterations increased with model size.

rows.subject: Pythia-1B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune on four-operand addition and track digit-wise error.
rows.value: The fine-tuned model prioritizes the most significant digit and retains the reverse learning order; it does not reach 100% accuracy within the stated budget.
rows.note: This reports a fine-tuning trajectory, not delayed generalization on realistic pretraining data.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.baseline: Standard training takes approximately 60,000 iterations to converge
rows.value: The model still exhibits reverse learning order; this format requires 10,000 iterations to reach convergence.
rows.locator: Figure 7(d), Figure 29(a); Section 5.3 and Appendix E.3
rows.note: Scratchpad supervision changes convergence speed but does not restore the human-like digit order.

rows.subject: NanoGPT (10.63M parameters)
rows.baseline: Standard training takes approximately 60,000 iterations to converge
rows.value: The most significant digit is learned first and the remaining three positions are learned nearly simultaneously; this format requires 1,000 iterations to reach convergence.
rows.locator: Figure 7(e), Figure 29(b); Section 5.3 and Appendix E.3
rows.note: The authors say the format does not recover a clean human-like learning order.

rows.subject: 10 open-source LLMs (aggregate reported)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate on clause-extended GSM8K questions with increasing numbers of added clauses.
rows.baseline: Accuracy at fewer added clauses; numeric baseline not stated
rows.value: All 10 evaluated models deteriorate as the number of added clauses increases.
rows.note: The paper evaluates already-trained models under an evaluation shift; it does not study delayed generalization during their training.
